Icelandic Krona Plummets Amid Currency Crisis, Disrupting Transport Sector and Isavia Ohf

Iceland is grappling with a deepening currency crisis as the krona's value plunged by over 30% against major currencies in the past three weeks, triggering supply chain disruptions, soaring import prices, and sharp declines in consumer spending. The economic shock is reverberating across sectors, with the transport and aviation industries particularly hard hit. Isavia Ohf, the country’s state-owned airport and air navigation operator, is among the companies reporting significant operational challenges as the crisis unfolds.

The krona’s collapse began in late May, following a wave of capital outflows amid investor concerns about mounting inflation and a widening current account deficit. The Central Bank of Iceland’s emergency interest rate hike to 10% last week has so far failed to halt the currency’s slide, and further policy measures are reportedly under consideration.

At Keflavik International Airport, managed by Isavia Ohf, officials are contending with immediate cost pressures. “Many of our contracts are denominated in euros or US dollars, and the krona’s depreciation has pushed our operating expenses up by nearly 40% in a matter of weeks,” said Björn Ólafsson, Isavia Ohf’s chief financial officer. “We’re working closely with partners and suppliers to manage cash flow and ensure continuity of critical services, but the situation is extremely challenging.”

The crisis is affecting passenger flows as well. Airline ticket prices have surged as carriers pass on higher costs, prompting a drop in both inbound tourism and outbound Icelandic travel. According to the Icelandic Travel Industry Association, advance bookings for July and August are down 18% year-on-year. “We’re seeing a sharp slowdown in the tourism sector, which is vital to Iceland’s economy,” said association spokesperson Elín Jónsdóttir. “The uncertainty is making it difficult for businesses to plan for the summer season.”

Freight operators are also struggling with the cost of imported spare parts and fuel. Guðni Haraldsson, managing director of the logistics company North Atlantic Freight, said, “We’re facing delays and price increases on essential goods, and some suppliers have temporarily suspended shipments until exchange rates stabilize.”

Trade unions have called for urgent government intervention to protect jobs and support vulnerable households. In a statement, the Federation of Icelandic Labour Unions urged the government to “act decisively to stabilize the financial system and prevent a wave of layoffs.”

While the government has signalled it is preparing a crisis response package, including support for key industries and measures to stabilize the krona, details have yet to be announced. For now, Iceland’s business community is bracing for continued volatility as the currency crisis threatens to deepen.
